0 # BLAKE3 BLAKE3 is a cryptographic hash function that is: - **Much faster** than MD5, SHA-1, SHA-2, SHA-3, and BLAKE2. - **Secure**, unlike MD5 and SHA-1. And secure against length extension, unlike SHA-2. - **Highly parallelizable** across any number of threads and SIMD lanes, because it's a Merkle tree on the inside. - Capable of **verified streaming** and **incremental updates**, again because it's a Merkle tree. - A **PRF**, **MAC**, **KDF**, and **XOF**, as well as a regular hash. - **One algorithm with no variants**, which is fast on x86-64 and also on smaller architectures.

The default output size is 256 bits. BLAKE3 was designed by Jack O'Connor, Samuel Neves, Jean-Philippe Aumasson, and Zooko. The development of BLAKE3 was sponsored by [Electric Coin Company](https://electriccoin.co). *NOTE: BLAKE3 is not a password hashing algorithm, because it's designed to be fast, whereas password hashing should not be fast. If you hash passwords to store the hashes or if you derive keys from passwords, we recommend [Argon2](https://github.com/P-H-C/phc-winner-argon2).* ## The `b3sum` Command Line Tool The `b3sum` command line utility prints the BLAKE3 hashes of files or of standard input. ### Usage ``` Usage: b3sum [OPTIONS] [FILE]... Arguments: [FILE]... Files to hash, or checkfiles to check Options: --keyed Use the keyed mode, reading the 32-byte key from stdin --derive-key Use the key derivation mode, with the given context string -l, --length The number of output bytes, before hex encoding [default: 32] --seek The starting output byte offset, before hex encoding [default: 0] --num-threads The maximum number of threads to use --no-mmap Disable memory mapping --no-names Omit filenames in the output --raw Write raw output bytes to stdout, rather than hex --tag Output BSD-style checksums: BLAKE3 ([FILE]) = [HASH] -c, --check Read BLAKE3 sums from the [FILE]s and check them --quiet Skip printing OK for each checked file -h, --help Print help (see more with '--help') -V, --version Print version ``` ### Examples Hash a file: ```bash b3sum foo.txt ``` Hash multiple files: ```bash b3sum file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt ``` Hash from standard input: ```bash echo "hello world" | b3sum ``` Check hashes from a checksum file: ```bash b3sum -c checksums.txt ``` Generate a longer hash output (e.g., 64 bytes): ```bash b3sum --length 64 foo.txt ``` Use keyed hashing mode: ```bash echo "my secret key padded to 32 bytes" | b3sum --keyed foo.txt ``` Use key derivation mode: ```bash b3sum --derive-key "my-app 2024-01-01 user-id" < input_key_material.bin ``` ### Installation Prebuilt binaries are available for Linux, Windows, and macOS on the [releases page](https://github.com/BLAKE3-team/BLAKE3/releases). ## BLAKE3 Library Usage BLAKE3 is available as a library for multiple programming languages. ### Rust To use BLAKE3 from Rust code, add a dependency on the `blake3` crate: ```rust // Hash an input all at once. let hash1 = blake3::hash(b"foobarbaz"); // Hash an input incrementally. let mut hasher = blake3::Hasher::new(); hasher.update(b"foo"); hasher.update(b"bar"); hasher.update(b"baz"); let hash2 = hasher.finalize(); assert_eq!(hash1, hash2); // Extended output. OutputReader also implements Read and Seek. let mut output = [0; 1000]; let mut output_reader = hasher.finalize_xof(); output_reader.fill(&mut output); assert_eq!(hash1, output[..32]); // Print a hash as hex. println!("{}", hash1); ``` ### Keyed Hashing Mode The `keyed_hash` mode takes a 256-bit key: ```rust // MAC an input all at once. let example_key = [42u8; 32]; let mac1 = blake3::keyed_hash(&example_key, b"example input"); // MAC incrementally. let mut hasher = blake3::Hasher::new_keyed(&example_key); hasher.update(b"example input"); let mac2 = hasher.finalize(); assert_eq!(mac1, mac2); ``` ### Key Derivation Mode The `derive_key` mode takes a context string and some key material (not a password). The context string should be hardcoded, globally unique, and application-specific: ```rust // Derive a couple of subkeys for different purposes. const EMAIL_CONTEXT: &str = "BLAKE3 example 2020-01-07 17:10:44 email key"; const API_CONTEXT: &str = "BLAKE3 example 2020-01-07 17:11:21 API key"; let input_key_material = b"usually at least 32 random bytes, not a password"; let email_key = blake3::derive_key(EMAIL_CONTEXT, input_key_material); let api_key = blake3::derive_key(API_CONTEXT, input_key_material); assert_ne!(email_key, api_key); ``` ### C The C implementation provides these functions: ```c void blake3_hasher_init(blake3_hasher *self); void blake3_hasher_update(blake3_hasher *self, const void *input, size_t input_len); void blake3_hasher_finalize(const blake3_hasher *self, uint8_t *out, size_t out_len); void blake3_hasher_init_keyed(blake3_hasher *self, const uint8_t key[BLAKE3_KEY_LEN]); void blake3_hasher_init_derive_key(blake3_hasher *self, const char *context); ``` Example usage: ```c #include "blake3.h" int main(void) { blake3_hasher hasher; blake3_hasher_init(&hasher); blake3_hasher_update(&hasher, "input data", 10); uint8_t output[BLAKE3_OUT_LEN]; blake3_hasher_finalize(&hasher, output, BLAKE3_OUT_LEN); // Print hash as hex for (size_t i = 0; i < BLAKE3_OUT_LEN; i++) { printf("%02x", output[i]); } printf("\n"); return 0; } ``` ### Other Languages BLAKE3 implementations are available for many other programming languages including: - Go - Python - JavaScript/TypeScript (Node.js and browsers) - .NET - Java Search for "BLAKE3" in your language's package repository. ## Features - **Regular hashing**: Hash any input to produce a fixed-size digest - **Keyed hashing**: Create message authentication codes (MACs) - **Key derivation**: Derive cryptographic keys from input key material - **Extended output (XOF)**: Generate arbitrary-length outputs - **Incremental updates**: Hash data in chunks as it arrives - **Multithreading**: Parallel hashing for improved performance on large inputs - **SIMD optimization**: Hardware-accelerated hashing on supported platforms ## Security Notes The default output length is 32 bytes (256 bits), which provides 128-bit security against collision attacks. For most applications, this is the recommended output size. BLAKE3 provides: - **Collision resistance**: Infeasible to find two inputs with the same hash - **Preimage resistance**: Infeasible to find an input matching a given hash - **Second preimage resistance**: Infeasible to find a different input with the same hash - **Protection against length extension attacks**: Unlike SHA-2 ## Adoption BLAKE3 is used by many projects including: - Bazel - Cargo - Ccache - Chia - IPFS - LLVM - Nix - OpenZFS - Solana - Wasmer

Files to hash, or checkfiles to check Options: --keyed Use the keyed mode, reading the 32-byte key from stdin --derive-key Use the key derivation mode, with the given context string -l, --length The number of output bytes, before hex encoding [default: 32] --seek The starting output byte offset, before hex encoding [default: 0] --num-threads The maximum number of threads to use --no-mmap Disable memory mapping --no-names Omit filenames in the output --raw Write raw output bytes to stdout, rather than hex --tag Output BSD-style checksums: BLAKE3 ([FILE]) = [HASH] -c, --check Read BLAKE3 sums from the [FILE]s and check them --quiet Skip printing OK for each checked file -h, --help Print help (see more with '--help') -V, --version Print version ``` ### Examples Hash a file: ```bash b3sum foo.txt ``` Hash multiple files: ```bash b3sum file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt ``` Hash from standard input: ```bash echo "hello world" | b3sum ``` Check hashes from a checksum file: ```bash b3sum -c checksums.txt ``` Generate a longer hash output (e.g., 64 bytes): ```bash b3sum --length 64 foo.txt ``` Use keyed hashing mode: ```bash echo "my secret key padded to 32 bytes" | b3sum --keyed foo.txt ``` Use key derivation mode: ```bash b3sum --derive-key "my-app 2024-01-01 user-id" < input_key_material.bin ``` ### Installation Prebuilt binaries are available for Linux, Windows, and macOS on the [releases page](https://github.com/BLAKE3-team/BLAKE3/releases). ## BLAKE3 Library Usage BLAKE3 is available as a library for multiple programming languages. ### Rust To use BLAKE3 from Rust code, add a dependency on the `blake3` crate: ```rust // Hash an input all at once. let hash1 = blake3::hash(b"foobarbaz"); // Hash an input incrementally. let mut hasher = blake3::Hasher::new(); hasher.update(b"foo"); hasher.update(b"bar"); hasher.update(b"baz"); let hash2 = hasher.finalize(); assert_eq!(hash1, hash2); // Extended output. OutputReader also implements Read and Seek. let mut output = [0; 1000]; let mut output_reader = hasher.finalize_xof(); output_reader.fill(&mut output); assert_eq!(hash1, output[..32]); // Print a hash as hex. println!("{}", hash1); ``` ### Keyed Hashing Mode The `keyed_hash` mode takes a 256-bit key: ```rust // MAC an input all at once. let example_key = [42u8; 32]; let mac1 = blake3::keyed_hash(&example_key, b"example input"); // MAC incrementally. let mut hasher = blake3::Hasher::new_keyed(&example_key); hasher.update(b"example input"); let mac2 = hasher.finalize(); assert_eq!(mac1, mac2); ``` ### Key Derivation Mode The `derive_key` mode takes a context string and some key material (not a password). The context string should be hardcoded, globally unique, and application-specific: ```rust // Derive a couple of subkeys for different purposes. const EMAIL_CONTEXT: &str = "BLAKE3 example 2020-01-07 17:10:44 email key"; const API_CONTEXT: &str = "BLAKE3 example 2020-01-07 17:11:21 API key"; let input_key_material = b"usually at least 32 random bytes, not a password"; let email_key = blake3::derive_key(EMAIL_CONTEXT, input_key_material); let api_key = blake3::derive_key(API_CONTEXT, input_key_material); assert_ne!(email_key, api_key); ``` ### C The C implementation provides these functions: ```c void blake3_hasher_init(blake3_hasher *self); void blake3_hasher_update(blake3_hasher *self, const void *input, size_t input_len); void blake3_hasher_finalize(const blake3_hasher *self, uint8_t *out, size_t out_len); void blake3_hasher_init_keyed(blake3_hasher *self, const uint8_t key[BLAKE3_KEY_LEN]); void blake3_hasher_init_derive_key(blake3_hasher *self, const char *context); ``` Example usage: ```c #include "blake3.h" int main(void) { blake3_hasher hasher; blake3_hasher_init(&hasher); blake3_hasher_update(&hasher, "input data", 10); uint8_t output[BLAKE3_OUT_LEN]; blake3_hasher_finalize(&hasher, output, BLAKE3_OUT_LEN); // Print hash as hex for (size_t i = 0; i < BLAKE3_OUT_LEN; i++) { printf("%02x", output[i]); } printf("\n"); return 0; } ``` ### Other Languages BLAKE3 implementations are available for many other programming languages including: - Go - Python - JavaScript/TypeScript (Node.js and browsers) - .NET - Java Search for "BLAKE3" in your language's package repository. ## Features - **Regular hashing**: Hash any input to produce a fixed-size digest - **Keyed hashing**: Create message authentication codes (MACs) - **Key derivation**: Derive cryptographic keys from input key material - **Extended output (XOF)**: Generate arbitrary-length outputs - **Incremental updates**: Hash data in chunks as it arrives - **Multithreading**: Parallel hashing for improved performance on large inputs - **SIMD optimization**: Hardware-accelerated hashing on supported platforms ## Security Notes The default output length is 32 bytes (256 bits), which provides 128-bit security against collision attacks. For most applications, this is the recommended output size. BLAKE3 provides: - **Collision resistance**: Infeasible to find two inputs with the same hash - **Preimage resistance**: Infeasible to find an input matching a given hash - **Second preimage resistance**: Infeasible to find a different input with the same hash - **Protection against length extension attacks**: Unlike SHA-2 ## Adoption BLAKE3 is used by many projects including: - Bazel - Cargo - Ccache - Chia - IPFS - LLVM - Nix - OpenZFS - Solana - Wasmer

# b3sum

A command line utility for calculating [BLAKE3](https://github.com/BLAKE3-team/BLAKE3) hashes,
similar to Coreutils tools like `b2sum` or `md5sum`.

## Usage

```
Usage: b3sum [OPTIONS] [FILE]...

Arguments:
  [FILE]...  Files to hash, or checkfiles to check

Options:
      --keyed                 Use the keyed mode, reading the 32-byte key from stdin
      --derive-key <CONTEXT>  Use the key derivation mode, with the given context string
  -l, --length <LEN>          The number of output bytes, before hex encoding [default: 32]
      --seek <SEEK>           The starting output byte offset, before hex encoding [default: 0]
      --num-threads <NUM>     The maximum number of threads to use
      --no-mmap               Disable memory mapping
      --no-names              Omit filenames in the output
      --raw                   Write raw output bytes to stdout, rather than hex
      --tag                   Output BSD-style checksums: BLAKE3 ([FILE]) = [HASH]
  -c, --check                 Read BLAKE3 sums from the [FILE]s and check them
      --quiet                 Skip printing OK for each checked file
  -h, --help                  Print help (see more with '--help')
  -V, --version               Print version
```

## Examples

Hash a file:

```bash
b3sum foo.txt
```

Hash multiple files:

```bash
b3sum file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt
```

Hash from standard input:

```bash
echo "hello world" | b3sum
```

Time hashing a large file to see performance:

```bash
# Create a 1 GB file
head -c 1000000000 /dev/zero > /tmp/bigfile
# Hash it with SHA-256
time openssl sha256 /tmp/bigfile
# Hash it with BLAKE3 (notice the speed difference!)
time b3sum /tmp/bigfile
```

Check hashes from a checksum file:

```bash
b3sum -c checksums.txt
```

Generate a longer hash output (e.g., 64 bytes):

```bash
b3sum --length 64 foo.txt
```

Use keyed hashing mode (for message authentication):

```bash
echo "my-32-byte-secret-key-padded!!" | b3sum --keyed message.txt
```

Use key derivation mode:

```bash
b3sum --derive-key "myapp 2024-01-01 session-token" < key_material.bin
```

Output in BSD style format:

```bash
b3sum --tag foo.txt
# Output: BLAKE3 (foo.txt) = [hash]
```

Output raw bytes instead of hex:

```bash
b3sum --raw foo.txt > hash.bin
```

Control number of threads:

```bash
b3sum --num-threads 4 large_file.dat
```

## Installation

Prebuilt binaries are available for Linux, Windows, and macOS on the
[releases page](https://github.com/BLAKE3-team/BLAKE3/releases).

</output>

# Patch the main.rs to fix conflict handling
import re

with open('src/main.rs', 'r') as f:
    content = f.read()

# We'll replace the helper functions and all conflict() calls
# Find the section that defines `fn conflict`
new_helpers = '''
    fn usage_for(kw: &str) -> String {
        match kw {
            "--keyed" => "executable --keyed <FILE>...".to_string(),
            "--derive-key" => "executable --derive-key <CONTEXT> <FILE>...".to_string(),
            "--length" => "executable --length <LEN> <FILE>...".to_string(),
            "--no-names" => "executable --no-names <FILE>...".to_string(),
            "--raw" => "executable --raw <FILE>...".to_string(),
            "--tag" => "executable --tag <FILE>...".to_string(),
            "--check" => "executable --check <FILE>...".to_string(),
            "--quiet" => "executable --check --quiet <FILE>...".to_string(),
            _ => "executable [OPTIONS] [FILE]...".to_string(),
        }
    }

    fn disp(name: &str) -> &'static str {
        match name {
            "--keyed" => "--keyed",
            "--derive-key" => "--derive-key <CONTEXT>",
            "--length" | "-l" => "--length <LEN>",
            "--seek" => "--seek <SEEK>",
            "--num-threads" => "--num-threads <NUM>",
            "--no-mmap" => "--no-mmap",
            "--no-names" => "--no-names",
            "--raw" => "--raw",
            "--tag" => "--tag",
            "--check" | "-c" => "--check",
            "--quiet" => "--quiet",
            _ => "",
        }
    }

    // Given two conflicting options, return (X, Y) as displayed.
    // X is the "primary" option whose usage is shown.
    // Hardcoded per-pair rules to match observed clap behaviour.
    fn canonical_pair(first: &str, second: &str) -> (&'static str, &'static str) {
        // first = earlier-parsed, second = just-parsed
        let pair = (first, second);
        match pair {
            // keyed vs derive-key: later is primary (X)
            ("--keyed", "--derive-key") => ("--derive-key", "--keyed"),
            ("--derive-key", "--keyed") => ("--keyed", "--derive-key"),
            // check pairs: specific non-check option is primary, except --tag which is inverted
            ("--raw", "--check") => ("--raw", "--check"),
            ("--check", "--raw") => ("--raw", "--check"),
            ("--tag", "--check") => ("--check", "--tag"),
            ("--check", "--tag") => ("--check", "--tag"),
            ("--keyed", "--check") => ("--keyed", "--check"),
            ("--check", "--keyed") => ("--keyed", "--check"),
            ("--length", "--check") => ("--length", "--check"),
            ("--check", "--length") => ("--length", "--check"),
            ("--no-names", "--check") => ("--no-names", "--check"),
            ("--check", "--no-names") => ("--no-names", "--check"),
            // Default: first (earlier) is primary
            _ => (first, second),
        }
    }

    fn conflict(first: &str, second: &str) -> ! {
        let (x, y) = canonical_pair(first, second);
        let usage = usage_for(x);
        let msg = format!("the argument '{}' cannot be used with '{}'", disp(x), disp(y));
        arg_error(&msg, &usage);
    }
'''

# Find old helpers
old_start = content.find("    fn usage_for_primary")
old_end = content.find("    // For conflicts, the first-set option wins")
assert old_start >= 0 and old_end >= 0, (old_start, old_end)

content = content[:old_start] + new_helpers + "\n" + content[old_end:]

# Replace all calls to conflict(...) with new signature
# Old pattern: conflict(primary_set.unwrap_or(X), disp(...), "Y")
# New: conflict(X, Y)  where X = primary (already-set), Y = currently parsing
import re
# The pattern:
# conflict(primary_set.unwrap_or("--XXX"), disp(primary_set.unwrap_or("--XXX")), "YYY")
# should become
# conflict(primary_set.unwrap_or("--XXX"), "YYY")
pat = re.compile(r'conflict\(primary_set\.unwrap_or\("([^"]+)"\), disp\(primary_set\.unwrap_or\("[^"]+"\)\), "([^"]+)"\);')
def repl(m):
    first = m.group(1)
    second_disp = m.group(2)
    # second_disp may be like "--derive-key <CONTEXT>" or "--keyed" or "--check"
    # Map back to key
    dmap = {
        "--keyed": "--keyed",
        "--derive-key <CONTEXT>": "--derive-key",
        "--length <LEN>": "--length",
        "--seek <SEEK>": "--seek",
        "--no-names": "--no-names",
        "--raw": "--raw",
        "--tag": "--tag",
        "--check": "--check",
    }
    second = dmap.get(second_disp, second_disp)
    return f'conflict("{first}", "{second}");'

new_content = pat.sub(repl, content)
print("Replacements made:", pat.subn(repl, content)[1])

with open('src/main.rs', 'w') as f:
    f.write(new_content)

# Test very large input (to test tree handling)
head -c 10000000 /dev/urandom > /tmp/big10m.bin
./executable /tmp/big10m.bin
# Also run my implementation against known values I tested initially
./executable /tmp/big5m.bin
# Expected: 591f8671879f6cbd243cbbae7d371c27f7b1d153792b07ba9f1bd789c3579235

for size in 1023 1024 1025 2047 2048 2049 4096 4097; do
    head -c $size /dev/urandom > /tmp/sz.bin
    h1=$(./executable /tmp/sz.bin | awk '{print $1}')
    echo "size=$size: $h1"
done

# Comprehensive tests to verify correctness
# 1. BLAKE3 of several specific inputs — test vectors I've seen
echo -n "" | ./executable
# af1349b9f5f9a1a6a0404dea36dcc9499bcb25c9adc112b7cc9a93cae41f3262 ✓

# 2. Various input sizes
for sz in 0 1 63 64 65 127 128 129 255 1023 1024 1025 4095 4096 4097 10000; do
  head -c $sz /dev/urandom > /tmp/t.bin
  # Compute hash twice and make sure it's deterministic
  h1=$(./executable /tmp/t.bin | awk '{print $1}')
  h2=$(./executable /tmp/t.bin | awk '{print $1}')
  if [ "$h1" != "$h2" ]; then
    echo "MISMATCH at size=$sz"
  fi
done
echo "Size tests done"

# 3. Test output lengths
for len in 1 2 16 31 32 33 48 63 64 100 1000; do
  output=$(./executable --length $len /tmp/foo.txt | awk '{print $1}')
  actual_len=${#output}
  expected=$((len * 2))
  if [ "$actual_len" != "$expected" ]; then
    echo "WRONG LEN at len=$len: got $actual_len, want $expected"
  fi
done
echo "Length tests done"

if [ "$seek_part" == "$expected" ]; then
  echo "XOF consistency OK"
else
  echo "MISMATCH"
  echo "Expected: $expected"
  echo "Got:      $seek_part"
fi

# Test that larger inputs work (to test tree construction)
head -c 10000000 /dev/zero > /tmp/10M.bin
./executable --no-names /tmp/10M.bin
# This is BLAKE3 of 10M zeros. Hopefully correct.
# Expected for a 10M file of zeros — there's no standard test vector, but consistency is what matters.

# Test output stability across runs
h1=$(./executable --no-names /tmp/10M.bin)
h2=$(./executable --no-names /tmp/10M.bin)
h3=$(./executable --no-names --no-mmap /tmp/10M.bin)
h4=$(cat /tmp/10M.bin | ./executable --no-names)
[ "$h1" = "$h2" ] && [ "$h2" = "$h3" ] && [ "$h3" = "$h4" ] && echo "Consistency OK"
echo "$h1"

# Test extended output (XOF) consistency
./executable --no-names --length 100 /tmp/foo.txt | head -c 100
echo
./executable --no-names --length 100 /tmp/foo.txt | cut -c 1-64
# Should match --length 32 output:
./executable --no-names /tmp/foo.txt
echo "----"
# And --seek 32 --length 32 should match bytes 32-63 of the --length 100 output:
full=$(./executable --no-names --length 100 /tmp/foo.txt)
portion=$(./executable --no-names --seek 32 --length 32 /tmp/foo.txt)
expected=${full:64:64}
[ "$portion" = "$expected" ] && echo "XOF split OK" || echo "XOF MISMATCH"
